texto:
Google is recruiting a Director+ level design leader to turn Discover into what its own job posting calls "a proactive, hyper-personalized concierge experience," offering a base salary of $275,000 to $382,000 plus a 30% bonus target and equity. The listing, titled Principal, UX, Search Discover, gained attention after Damien Andell, co-founder of the Discover research firm 1492.vision, highlighted it in a LinkedIn post on October 11, 2026.
In Short
Google posted a senior job opening for someone to redesign Discover, the news and video feed people see in the Google app, so that it anticipates what each person wants and helps them act on it. Discover sends most of the Google traffic that news sites receive, so any redesign affects publishers, creators and advertisers who buy ads in the feed. The posting describes a plan rather than a launched product, but it shows Google intends to push more AI formats into the feed while keeping human sources visible.
What the posting says
The listing sits on Google Careers under the title Principal, UX, Search Discover. It is marked Director+ and lists two locations, Mountain View, California, and New York. The posting does not carry a visible publication date; the version captured for this article was saved on October 12, 2026.
Its summary paragraph is blunt about the direction. According to Google, "As the Principal UX Lead for Discover, you will drive the UX strategy and execution for transforming Discover into a proactive, hyper-personalized feed. You will lead strategic design initiatives to redefine feed interactions, content formats, and AI-driven exploration experiences."
Three phrases in that passage carry most of the weight. "Proactive" points to a feed that acts before a user asks. "Hyper-personalized" goes beyond the interest signals Discover already uses. And "AI-driven exploration experiences" places AI at the centre of how people move through the feed, rather than as a single card type sitting among articles.
The responsibilities section repeats and sharpens the idea. The first listed duty reads: "Lead the design vision and execution to transform Discover into a proactive, hyper-personalized concierge experience that helps users make progress on their goals. Balance AI capabilities while centering human voices and sources."
A concierge does things on someone's behalf. Framing Discover that way is a departure from its long-standing role as a passive, query-free stream of articles and videos. The second responsibility adds a related goal: to help "existing users go deeper, moving seamlessly from inspiration to action." The third describes how: "Evolve feed formats by scaling AI enabled formats, designing new engagement mechanisms, and elevating human voices and perspectives in the feed."
The remaining two duties are more conventional. One asks the hire to draw on experience with "scaled consumer feed products" to set best practices, and the other covers building "a high-craft design organization" that can "innovate to deliver native app interactions."
Who the role works with
The posting lists internal partners. According to Google, the hire "will partner closely with executive leadership across Product Management, Engineering, Data Science, UX Research, and cross-organization partners (YouTube, Shopping, Chrome, and Android) to deliver a unified experience."
The partner list is informative in its own right. YouTube already supplies a large share of what appears in Discover. Chrome hosts Discover on its mobile new tab page, and Android carries it in the Google app. Shopping is the newer element, and it sits naturally next to the phrase "from inspiration to action." The posting does not say what action means. Purchases, bookings, saving an item or following a creator would all fit the wording; Google gives no specifics.
Pay and seniority
Google published a base salary range for US candidates of $275,000 to $382,000, "+ 30% bonus target + equity + benefits." At the top of the band, a 30% bonus target would add $114,600, for target cash compensation of $496,600 before equity. The posting notes that individual pay depends on "job-related skills, experience, and relevant education or training," and that equity is granted at the discretion of Alphabet's board.
The minimum qualifications set a high bar. Google asks for a bachelor's degree in design, human-computer interaction, computer science or a related field, or equivalent experience; 15 years of experience "managing, scaling, and developing UX organizations in global technology organizations"; seven years of collaboration with executive partners across product, engineering, research and data science; and "Experience leading design for consumer feeds."
That last requirement narrows the field considerably. Few companies run consumer feeds at Discover's scale. Google has said Discover serves more than 800 million monthly active users, a figure reported when Google Ads app campaigns first gained access to Discover inventory in August 2019.
The preferred qualifications
The preferred qualifications reveal more about the agenda than the minimums do. Google lists four.
The first is experience "advocating ofr AI-native design tools and rapid prototyping methods (e.g., AI Studio, vibe coding) to accelerate team exploration and design velocity." The typo ("ofr") appears in the posting as published, as does "expeirence" in the minimum qualifications. The reference to vibe coding and to Google's own AI Studio indicates that the design team itself is expected to prototype with generative AI tools.
The second is executive communication. The third and fourth are the ones that matter most outside Google. The posting seeks "Demonstrated success leading cross-product area initiatives, unifying personalization frameworks, and building creator/publisher value exchanges." And it asks for a "Proven track record of defining product strategy for youth demographics and driving product-market fit in competitive content ecosystems."
Unifying personalization frameworks suggests that personalization logic currently differs across Google products and that the role is expected to help consolidate it. Creator/publisher value exchanges is the most direct reference to the people whose work fills the feed. The phrase implies a deliberate design of what publishers and creators get in return for supplying content; the posting does not say whether that means traffic, revenue, audience data or something else. Youth demographics points to a competitive concern. The posting names no rival, but "competitive content ecosystems" leaves little doubt that Discover is measured against short-video and social feeds that draw younger audiences.
How the listing surfaced
The posting reached a wider audience through Andell, whose LinkedIn profile describes him as co-founder of 1492.vision, a Google Discover researcher and a Google Bug Hunter. His post, timestamped 18 hours before it was captured on the morning of October 12, 2026, opened: "Google wants to transform Google Discover into a proactive, hyper-personalized feed."
Andell summarised the responsibilities and singled out one line. "One line is explicit: balance AI capabilities while centering human voices and sources," he wrote. He also flagged the preferred qualifications on personalization frameworks and creator/publisher value exchanges, adding that "Youth demographics are mentioned too."
In the comments, Virginie Clève, a digital strategist who describes herself as a Google News and Discover specialist, called it "Excellent Intel." Andell replied that "articles on 1492 are coming soon with lots of info on the latest Google Discover features." Metehan Yeşilyurt, a GEO researcher at Peec AI, wrote "Great sleuth!" The post had 27 reactions at the time of capture.
Andell has a track record of surfacing unannounced Discover changes. In April 2026 he spotted a "You asked to see" label on Discover cards tied to the beta Tailor Your Feed chat. In May 2026, he and Sylvain Deaure of 1492.vision documented a pilot that gave 54 US publishers enhanced Discover profiles, identified among 46,926 monitored publishers. And in September 2026 he found four configuration flags covering AI summary cards after Google began testing a "Dive deeper" button.
A feed already moving in this direction
Read against the past 13 months of Discover changes, the posting reads less as a new direction than as a statement of where several separate tests are heading.
In September 2025, Google began adding posts from X and Instagram, plus YouTube Shorts, to Discover and introduced a follow feature giving each followed publisher or creator a dedicated space. That change is the most obvious precedent for "elevating human voices and perspectives in the feed." In February 2026, the February 2026 Discover core update set out to reduce clickbait, favour locally relevant sites and surface topic expertise. Then, on June 4, 2026, Google launched Search profiles in the United States, letting eligible publishers and creators pin up to eight posts and add up to eight links.
Personalization controls have moved in parallel. Preferred Sources, first applied to Top Stories, was extended into AI Overviews and AI Mode on May 27, 2026. By August 20, 2026, Google said more than 600,000 unique sources had been selected, and described free-text tuning for Discover as arriving within days. The Tailor Your Feed chat, which lets users describe in plain language what they want more of, is the closest existing feature to a "concierge."
The AI side has grown just as quickly. Marfeel data from December 2025 found that AI Summaries filled 51% of Discover feed positions in the US, Brazil and Mexico, with 77% of US AI Summaries defaulting to inline YouTube plays. On September 18, 2026, Robby Stein, Google's vice president of product for Search, said Google was testing the "Dive deeper" button, which opens a topic overview rather than a publisher page. The posting's phrase "AI-driven exploration experiences" describes that kind of feature closely.
The tension in one sentence
The instruction to "Balance AI capabilities while centering human voices and sources" sits at the centre of the publisher debate. Generated summaries and topic overviews keep readers inside Google's surfaces. Human sources are where the reporting comes from. The posting treats the two as compatible goals to be balanced; publishers have measured the trade-off in lost clicks.
Why this matters for publishers and marketers
Discover's commercial weight explains why a single job listing drew attention. NewzDash data covering more than 400 publishers showed Discover's share of Google traffic to news sites rising from 37.03% in 2023 to 67.51% in the fourth quarter of 2025, while Google Web Search fell from 51.10% to 27.42%. An August 2025 analysis of Chartbeat data covering 2,000 sites had already found Discover accounting for two-thirds of Google referrals to news and media sites.
For publishers who now depend on Discover more than on search, a redesign aimed at a "proactive, hyper-personalized concierge" raises practical questions. Will a concierge model send readers to source pages, or resolve their interest inside Google? How will "creator/publisher value exchanges" be defined, and by whom? The posting answers neither. It also says nothing about whether publishers will gain new controls, beyond the profiles and Preferred Sources tools already in place.
Measurement is a separate concern. Discover data in Search Console has had repeated logging problems in 2026, including a May 21, 2026 incident that wiped a day of Discover clicks and impressions. New AI formats and concierge-style interactions would add new kinds of engagement that existing reports may not capture.
Advertisers have a direct stake too. Demand Gen campaigns serve image and video ads in Discover alongside YouTube, Gmail and Maps. If feed formats change to "scaling AI enabled formats" and new "engagement mechanisms," the placements around which those ads appear will change with them. A Shopping partnership and an "inspiration to action" mandate would make Discover more relevant to commerce advertisers, though Google has not announced any ad product tied to this work.
The pattern resembles shifts elsewhere in Google Search. AI Overviews and AI Mode moved answers above or in place of links; the Discover posting signals a similar ambition for the feed that has become publishers' largest source of Google traffic.
What the posting does not establish
A job listing is not a product roadmap. It describes the remit of one senior hire, and Google has not published a timeline, a feature list or a market rollout for a concierge Discover. Job descriptions are also written to attract candidates, and ambitious language is common in them. Google has made no public statement on the listing, and the posting itself names no launch.
Still, the wording is specific. The listing names partner teams, sets requirements around consumer feeds, personalization, creator and publisher economics and younger users, and uses the word "proactive" twice. Taken with the tests Andell and others have documented, it is a reasonable indication of the direction Google's Search organisation has set for Discover.

Summary
Who: Google, through a Google Careers listing for a Principal, UX, Search Discover role at Director+ level; Damien Andell of 1492.vision, who highlighted it on LinkedIn; and the publishers, creators and advertisers who depend on Discover.
What: Google is hiring a design leader to transform Discover into "a proactive, hyper-personalized concierge experience," scale AI-enabled formats, center human voices and sources, unify personalization frameworks and build creator/publisher value exchanges, with a US base salary of $275,000 to $382,000 plus a 30% bonus target and equity.
When: Andell's LinkedIn post appeared on October 11, 2026; the listing was live on October 12, 2026. The posting carries no publication date and gives no product timeline.
Where: The role is based in Mountain View, California, or New York, and works with YouTube, Shopping, Chrome and Android teams. Discover appears in the Google app, on Chrome's mobile new tab page and on the mobile Google.com homepage.
Why: Discover has become the largest source of Google traffic for news publishers, and Google is already testing AI summaries, topic overviews and plain-language feed tuning. The posting sets out the direction those experiments point to, with consequences for referral traffic, measurement and ad placements in the feed.
